touches.text: Instance: every device has at least one; a singleton is instance 0.
Two callers waking the same part at once start only one: the part that binds its socket first is the only one; a second copy finds it taken and exits quietly (as the ground loop does, 5.6.4.3).

Akien 2026-11-13, said in akiendell's session, answering the same Q#93 on a second asking (verbatim): "no there's no conflict there. those are completely different kinds of things. spinning up a second ground loop should see the first, and that it's fine, and exit quietly. if we're starting a new one on purpose, like there's an older one running, we'll add --force, which means kill the old one. we change that intention. i have no recollection why it says loudly. but the naming, yes. if we had two zeros how would messages get routed? or <host>_cc_RESCUE? we DO want to be able to spin up more than one of something. many things can be singletons or not... like the embeddings generator. if we wound up with too much traffic, we might open a second on another host. but the launcher has to ask the shim to create the instance, and so it's the shim's job to say 'we've been asked to start and instance, then we've not been given a name for it, then we have a cc_0 instance, so I'll launch it with cc_1'"

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.

An instance is declared by its folder existing in class-space: cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/ (one address in two roots). Declared = the folders (read by the rack tool, 17.20); running = which of those are in the rack.

Every device has a shim. Each shim is its own process, one per instance, and connects to the bus as a client. WHY: in the bus process, updating one shim meant bringing the whole bus down, and one shim's stall was everyone's. Separate, a shim restarts itself when its own files change, like the ground loop, and the bus stays up.
The shim always starts its device. Nothing else does.
